title: Episode 30: VS Code Accessibility Reference
description: Complete accessibility settings, audio signals, diff viewer, and screen reader configs.
concepts: editor.accessibilitySupport setting and what it controls
Screen reader mode indicators and behavior changes
Audio cues: what each sound means and how to configure them
Accessibility announcements: text-based status updates for screen readers
The Accessible Diff Viewer: navigating code changes by keyboard
Terminal accessibility: screen reader support in the integrated terminal
High contrast themes and zoom levels
Keyboard-only navigation: all the shortcuts that matter
Troubleshooting accessibility issues: common problems and fixes
transcriptText:
[ALEX]
Welcome back. This time we’re doing something a little different. Think of this as your technical field guide for making Visual Studio Code work well if you use a screen reader, have low vision, or just want a more accessible setup for coding, reviewing diffs, using Git, and working with Copilot.

[JAMIE]
So not just a beginner tour.

[ALEX]
Right. More like a reference lesson in conversation form. The appendix behind this episode is meant to be a lookup manual. It even recommends practical ways to jump around it: Go to Line with Control+G, Go to Symbol with Control+Shift+O, and bookmarking the file in VS Code with Control+K, then Control+K so you can reopen it fast later.

[JAMIE]
That’s helpful because reference files can be long, and long can feel intimidating.

[ALEX]
Exactly. And the appendix is explicit about different access strategies. For screen reader users, it treats the file as something you navigate structurally. For low vision users, it suggests bumping font size with Control+Equals before scanning long tables, using orientation aids like breadcrumbs or the minimap if that helps, and using high contrast themes so tables and inline code are easier to distinguish. For sighted users, it points to the table of contents links and the outline view with Control+Shift+O.

[JAMIE]
I like that it doesn’t assume one kind of learner.

[ALEX]
And one more administrative note: this appendix is a companion reference to the main VS Code setup and accessibility chapters, and it points to the official VS Code accessibility docs as the authoritative source.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Let’s start with the main settings you’ll actually tune. In VS Code, accessibility settings can be changed in the Settings interface with Control+Comma, or directly in settings dot json through the Command Palette by opening User Settings JSON.

[JAMIE]
Can we separate the settings into categories that matter in practice?

[ALEX]
Yes. Core editor behavior, diff and merge behavior, terminal behavior, and announcement or notification behavior.

[JAMIE]
Let’s do core editor behavior first.

[ALEX]
The most important setting is editor dot accessibilitySupport. Its values are auto, on, and off. Auto tries to detect screen readers like NVDA, JAWS, or VoiceOver. On forces screen reader optimizations. Off disables them.

[JAMIE]
And if detection is flaky?

[ALEX]
Then forcing it to on is often the right move.

[JAMIE]
What else matters right away?

[ALEX]
Editor dot accessibilityPageSize controls how many lines are read with page navigation in screen reader mode. Default is ten. That sounds minor, but it changes how much content you hear at a time.

[JAMIE]
So it’s part comfort, part efficiency.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Then there are several visual guide settings, like bracket pair guides, horizontal bracket guides, active bracket highlighting, indentation highlighting, and indentation guides. These are mainly visual. The appendix’s message is clear: for screen reader users, many of these aren’t useful and may just add visual complexity for mixed workflows.

[JAMIE]
So if I’m blind and not using that visual information, I can simplify.

[ALEX]
Yes. Similarly, editor dot minimap dot enabled is visual only, and the recommendation is to turn it off for screen reader users. Editor dot renderWhitespace is also important. The recommended value for screen readers is none, because hearing code is hard enough without trying to manage a UI designed to show whitespace visually.

[JAMIE]
What about line wrapping?

[ALEX]
Editor dot wordWrap is recommended on for screen reader users, especially with long lines. It can reduce horizontal navigation friction. And workbench dot editor dot enablePreview is worth considering too. If preview mode stays on, opening files can reuse one tab. Turning it off means files open in persistent tabs, which many users find easier to track.

[JAMIE]
And hover popups?

[ALEX]
Editor dot hover dot enabled can stay on, but the key point is this: for accessible reading of hover content, use Accessible View with Alt+F2.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now diffs. This matters a lot for GitHub learners.

[ALEX]
It really does. A few settings make a huge difference. DiffEditor dot diffAlgorithm should generally be advanced. The appendix specifically says it tends to produce better hunks for screen reader users.

[JAMIE]
Meaning more sensible blocks of changes.

[ALEX]
Right. DiffEditor dot ignoreTrimWhitespace should usually stay true. That reduces noise from whitespace-only changes. DiffEditor dot renderSideBySide is a major one: the visual default is true, but for screen readers the recommendation is false, which gives you inline diffs.

[JAMIE]
Why is inline better?

[ALEX]
Because you hear one stream of content with change markers, instead of trying to mentally coordinate two columns. DiffEditor dot wordWrap can also be turned on for long lines. And merge conflict decorators are visual helpers, but the appendix nudges screen reader users toward the Accessible Diff workflow instead.

[JAMIE]
So if I remember only one thing: inline diffs, advanced algorithm, ignore trim whitespace.

[ALEX]
That’s an excellent practical summary.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
The terminal has its own accessibility settings. Terminal dot integrated dot screenReaderMode can be auto, on, or off, parallel to editor accessibility support. Terminal dot integrated dot enableBell is recommended on if you want audio feedback. Terminal dot integrated dot accessibleViewFocusesTerminal controls whether focus returns to the terminal after closing Accessible View, and by default it does. Terminal dot integrated dot accessibleViewPreserveCursorPosition controls whether your cursor position is preserved when opening Accessible View.

[JAMIE]
That’s subtle, but I can imagine it matters if you’re reading command output and then want to continue right where you left off.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Small settings, big effect on rhythm.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
And then there’s the verbosity layer.

[ALEX]
Yes. A whole group of accessibility dot verbosity settings controls whether VS Code announces context in particular parts of the interface. The appendix lists comments, the diff editor, the main editor, hover, inline chat, inline completions, the keybindings editor, notebooks, panel chat, the settings editor, and the terminal.

[JAMIE]
So if something feels too chatty, or too quiet, this is where I tune it.

[ALEX]
Exactly. And that leads naturally into audio cues, because accessible feedback in VS Code isn’t just speech.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Audio cues provide nonverbal feedback through sound. You can get to those settings by opening Settings with Control+Comma and searching for audio cue, or by editing settings dot json directly.

[JAMIE]
And each cue has the same value choices, right?

[ALEX]
Yes: auto, on, and off. Auto means play the sound only in screen reader mode. On means always play it. Off means never.

[JAMIE]
What kinds of events can have sounds attached?

[ALEX]
A lot. The appendix lists a broad set of accessibility signals. Some are about terminal or output actions, like clear. Some are tied to Copilot chat, including when a request is sent, while a response is pending, and when a response is received. Some are about debugging, like hitting a breakpoint or landing on a line with a breakpoint. Several are specific to diff navigation, including sounds for deleted, inserted, and modified lines. Others signal formatting completion, errors, warnings, folded areas, inline suggestions, unavailable inlay hints, and notebook events.

[JAMIE]
So this is really a sensory feedback system, not just a convenience feature.

[ALEX]
Exactly. And the recommendations in the appendix are practical. Important state changes, like a line with an error or a completed chat response, are often recommended on. Some lower-priority cues are auto, and a few are off if they tend to add little value.

[JAMIE]
Can users change the sounds themselves?

[ALEX]
Yes, the appendix includes customization of signal sounds, including sound file requirements. The big idea is that if you do customize, use supported audio files and keep them short, distinct, and easy to recognize. You want cues that clarify, not cues that become a second source of clutter.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let’s get into the Accessible Diff Viewer, because that’s probably one of the most important workflows for Git and pull request review.

[ALEX]
I agree. The appendix gives a complete guide. First, when should you use it? Any time the standard visual diff is hard to interpret with a screen reader, when you want a text-forward representation of changes, or when navigating code review changes line by line would be easier than trying to understand two-pane layout.

[JAMIE]
How do you open it?

[ALEX]
The appendix emphasizes the accessible diff workflow and points to function-key navigation, especially F7, as part of moving through changes. In practice, you use the diff tools built into VS Code and then switch to the accessible representation designed for screen reader reading.

[JAMIE]
And once it opens, what is its structure like?

[ALEX]
At the top level, it’s organized to present changed content as understandable text rather than as a visual comparison grid. One concept the appendix calls out is line prefixes. Those prefixes indicate what kind of change you’re hearing or reading: added, deleted, modified, or context. That labeling is essential because it replaces the color and spatial layout sighted users rely on.

[JAMIE]
So the prefixes are the semantic anchors.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Then there are hunks. A hunk is a block of related changes. That’s the unit you navigate. Instead of thinking, I’m moving through the entire file visually, think, I’m moving through meaningful clusters of edits.

[JAMIE]
That sounds more cognitively manageable.

[ALEX]
It usually is. The appendix also talks about navigating hunks and about screen reader-specific navigation differences. For NVDA and JAWS, the workflow often depends on browse mode versus focus mode and using heading or structural navigation appropriately. For VoiceOver on macOS, navigation conventions differ, so users rely on VoiceOver’s own reading and interaction commands.

[JAMIE]
And what are context lines in this setup?

[ALEX]
Context lines are unchanged lines included around the edits to help you understand where a change happened. They answer the question, what was around this edit before and after? The appendix even gives an example to reinforce that changed lines without surrounding context can be hard to interpret.

[JAMIE]
So context is not noise. It’s orientation.

[ALEX]
Exactly right.

[JAMIE]
And then the big comparison: inline versus side by side.

[ALEX]
Yes. The appendix is explicit. Inline diff view is recommended for screen readers. Side by side is the default visual presentation and works well if you can compare columns visually, but it’s much harder in speech output. So to switch to inline view, set diffEditor dot renderSideBySide to false.

[JAMIE]
That one setting keeps coming up for good reason.

[ALEX]
It really does. And the appendix includes learning-card style reminders for the accessible diff viewer, reinforcing when to use it, how to think in hunks, and why inline structure is friendlier for nonvisual review.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Next, the appendix gets very specific about screen reader configurations.

[JAMIE]
Which I appreciate, because “it supports screen readers” is not the same as “here’s how to make your screen reader and editor cooperate.”

[ALEX]
Exactly. For NVDA, it includes recommended NVDA settings, mentions NVDA add-ons that may help with VS Code, and highlights VS Code-specific NVDA commands.

[JAMIE]
Without assuming everyone uses the same add-ons.

[ALEX]
Right. The point is not that every user must install extras, but that VS Code users often benefit from checking whether speech modes, punctuation levels, browse-versus-focus behavior, and any editor-friendly add-ons align with coding work.

[JAMIE]
And JAWS?

[ALEX]
Similarly, it covers recommended JAWS settings, JAWS scripts for VS Code, and VS Code-specific JAWS commands. That matters because JAWS users may depend more heavily on custom scripts in some environments, and because verbosity and cursor behavior can shape the coding experience dramatically.

[JAMIE]
Then VoiceOver on macOS gets its own configuration section.

[ALEX]
Yes. The appendix includes recommended VoiceOver Utility settings, VS Code-specific VoiceOver commands, and Quick Nav navigation when Quick Nav is enabled. That last part matters because Quick Nav changes how arrow keys behave, and in a code editor that can significantly affect movement and interaction.

[JAMIE]
So the general lesson is: don’t just tweak VS Code. Tune the screen reader and the editor together.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Accessibility is an ecosystem, not a single checkbox.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now for the part many learners want as a cheat sheet: keyboard shortcuts.

[ALEX]
The appendix organizes them by task. Let’s walk through the categories rather than pretending one giant list is memorable all at once.

[JAMIE]
Please.

[ALEX]
Global navigation includes the commands that help you move around VS Code itself: Command Palette, settings, quick open, outline and symbol navigation, and panel focus changes. These are the shortcuts that reduce hunting.

[JAMIE]
Then sidebar panels.

[ALEX]
Right. Explorer, Search, Source Control, Run and Debug, Extensions, and related panel focus commands. For accessibility, knowing how to jump directly to a panel is better than tabbing through unpredictable interface layers.

[JAMIE]
What about file work in the editor?

[ALEX]
Editor file operations include opening files, saving, saving all, closing, reopening, and managing tabs. Combined with turning preview tabs off, these shortcuts make file handling more stable.

[JAMIE]
And navigation inside files?

[ALEX]
That’s its own category: go to line, go to symbol, move by word, move by line, page movement, and other cursor travel commands. If you’re reading code nonvisually, navigation fluency is everything.

[JAMIE]
Editing is separate from navigation.

[ALEX]
Yes. Editor editing includes line manipulation, indentation, commenting, duplicating, deleting, and formatting. Then there’s find and replace, which is especially important in large files and long markdown documents.

[JAMIE]
And multi-cursor?

[ALEX]
Included too. Powerful, but not always the first tool a screen reader user reaches for. Still, the appendix treats it as part of complete coverage.

[JAMIE]
Terminal shortcuts must be in there.

[ALEX]
Yes, along with Source Control and Git shortcuts, diff viewer shortcuts, Copilot shortcuts, accessibility feature shortcuts, Problems panel shortcuts, and Markdown preview shortcuts.

[JAMIE]
That’s a lot of ground.

[ALEX]
It is, but the categories matter because they mirror real workflows. For example, a Git review flow might involve Explorer, editor navigation, Source Control, diff viewer movement, and Problems panel checks. A writing flow might lean on editor commands, markdown preview, and find and replace. A Copilot-heavy flow adds inline completions and panel chat navigation.

[JAMIE]
So the appendix is not just listing keys. It’s mapping the terrain.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Then there’s a deeper section on accessibility signals types and customization.

[JAMIE]
How is that different from the earlier audio cues list?

[ALEX]
Earlier, we talked about what cues exist. Here, the appendix expands into how signals behave as a system: announcement verbosity settings, custom announcement timing, and signal priorities.

[JAMIE]
Let’s unpack that.

[ALEX]
Announcement verbosity means deciding how much spoken context VS Code gives in different parts of the interface. If you’re overwhelmed, reduce verbosity in the places where you already know the pattern. If you miss important context, increase it.

[JAMIE]
And timing?

[ALEX]
Custom announcement timing is about when feedback occurs and whether it arrives at moments that interrupt you or moments that support you. Some users want immediate cues. Others want fewer interruptions and more manual access through Accessible View.

[JAMIE]
Signal priorities sounds like triage.

[ALEX]
That’s a good way to think about it. Not every event deserves equal prominence. Errors, completed responses, and change-type indicators in diffs may be high priority. Less important status information can be downgraded to auto or off. The appendix’s learning cards on accessibility signals reinforce that the goal is usable feedback, not maximum feedback.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
That sets us up for the settings dot json profiles.

[ALEX]
Yes, and these are very practical. The appendix offers example configurations for different working styles.

[JAMIE]
Let’s go one by one.

[ALEX]
First is a minimal screen reader profile. This is for users who prefer fewer announcements and who open Accessible View manually when needed. The philosophy is low noise, deliberate reading.

[JAMIE]
So maybe a strong fit for experienced users who don’t want constant narration.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Second is a maximum feedback profile for users who want all audio and verbal announcements. That’s especially helpful when you’re learning the interface or want confirmation for many actions.

[JAMIE]
Then there’s a Copilot-optimized profile.

[ALEX]
Right. That one emphasizes settings useful for GitHub Copilot workflows, like announcing inline completions and chat activity, and making AI interactions easier to track nonvisually.

[JAMIE]
And a Git or diff-optimized profile.

[ALEX]
Yes. That profile is for heavy pull request review and diff work. It would center the accessible diff experience: inline diffs, strong diff signals, and settings that reduce review noise, such as ignoring trim whitespace.

[JAMIE]
Then performance-optimized.

[ALEX]
For slower machines or very large repositories. The idea there is that accessibility also includes responsiveness. Turning off visually rich or nonessential features can make the editor lighter and easier to use.

[JAMIE]
And then there’s a quick-copy balanced setup.

[ALEX]
Yes. The appendix includes a complete recommended settings block that you can paste into settings dot json for a balanced screen reader profile. The intent is not “one true setup,” but a solid baseline you can customize.

[JAMIE]
Which is reassuring, because people sometimes think accessibility settings are pass or fail.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Better to think in profiles and tradeoffs.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
The appendix also includes an update section for VS Code 1.120, focused on chat, the Agents window, and markdown diff updates.

[JAMIE]
So this is where the reference acknowledges that the tool keeps changing.

[ALEX]
Right. It covers what changed, then breaks the implications into three workflows: screen reader, low vision, and sighted.

[JAMIE]
What’s the practical takeaway?

[ALEX]
For screen reader users, the takeaway is to reevaluate chat and agent workflows whenever VS Code adds new panes or interaction models. You may need to check focus movement, verbosity settings, and whether Accessible View gives you a better way to read generated content.

[JAMIE]
And for low vision users?

[ALEX]
Consider how the newer chat and agent surfaces present dense information, whether scaling, contrast, or layout adjustments are needed, and whether markdown diff improvements make review easier. If markdown diffs become more readable, that can matter a lot in documentation-heavy repositories.

[JAMIE]
And sighted workflows are included too, even though this appendix centers accessibility.

[ALEX]
Yes, because accessibility references still need to explain the visual defaults that many teams assume. The section also includes settings references tied to those newer features, so learners know where to look when behavior changes after an update.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before we close, I want to ask about the table of contents and source map material. People often skip those.

[ALEX]
They shouldn’t. The table of contents is part of accessibility because navigation is accessibility. It tells you the reference is organized into settings, audio cues, accessible diff viewer, screen reader configurations, keyboard shortcuts, accessibility signals, configuration examples, and the newer 1.120 updates. That mental map lowers cognitive load.

[JAMIE]
And the authoritative sources?

[ALEX]
Also important. The appendix points to the official VS Code accessibility documentation as the primary authority, and then includes a section-level source map. Even if the extracted list in our source snapshot is messy, the purpose is clear: this reference is meant to be traceable and maintainable, so learners can verify details against official documentation when VS Code evolves.

[JAMIE]
So the document is both a learning tool and a maintenance-minded reference.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Can you give us a practical closing setup recommendation? Not a giant JSON block, just the decision points.

[ALEX]
Absolutely. If you use a screen reader in VS Code, start by forcing accessibility support on if auto detection is unreliable. Turn minimap off. Set word wrap on. Set whitespace rendering to none. Turn preview tabs off if you want steadier file tracking. For diffs, use the advanced diff algorithm, ignore trim whitespace, and switch to inline diff view. In the terminal, keep screen reader mode on or auto, and consider enabling the bell. Then tune verbosity and audio cues based on whether you prefer minimal interruption or rich feedback.

[JAMIE]
And if I’m doing a lot of Git review?

[ALEX]
Build around the Accessible Diff Viewer. Think in hunks, rely on line prefixes, keep context lines, and use inline rather than side-by-side comparison. That one workflow can make pull request review dramatically more usable.

[JAMIE]
And if I’m still learning?

[ALEX]
Choose the maximum-feedback end of the spectrum first, then reduce noise gradually as you build confidence.

[JAMIE]
That’s a great rule.

[ALEX]
And maybe the most important one. Accessible setup is iterative. You’re not trying to discover the perfect editor in one session. You’re trying to build a working environment that tells you what matters, stays quiet about what doesn’t, and supports the way you actually code.

[JAMIE]
That’s it for this reference conversation. Keep the appendix handy, treat it like a manual, and come back to it when your workflow changes.

[ALEX]
And when VS Code updates, check your assumptions. Accessibility features are improving, but the best setup is still the one you verify in practice.

# Appendix G: VS Code Accessibility Reference
>
> **Listen to Episode 30:** [VS Code Accessibility Reference](https://lp.csedesigns.com/ggg/PODCASTS.html) - a conversational audio overview of this chapter. Listen before reading to preview the concepts, or after to reinforce what you learned.

> **Reference companion to:** [Chapter 11: VS Code Interface](11-vscode-interface.md) | Also relevant: [Chapter 12](12-vscode-accessibility.md)
>
> **Authoritative source:** [VS Code Docs: Accessibility](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/editor/accessibility)

## Complete Technical Reference for Screen Reader Users

> **Purpose:** This appendix provides comprehensive technical documentation for all VS Code accessibility features, settings, and keyboard shortcuts. The main chapters cover essentials; this appendix is your complete reference manual.
>
> **Referenced by:** [VS Code Setup & Accessibility Basics](11-vscode-interface.md), [GitHub Copilot](16-github-copilot.md)

### Learning Cards: VS Code Accessibility Reference Overview

<details>
<summary>Screen reader users</summary>

- This appendix is your lookup manual -- use `Ctrl+G` (Go to Line) or `Ctrl+Shift+O` (Go to Symbol) to jump directly to a setting name
- Every table is structured with headers; use `T` in browse mode to jump between tables, then arrow through rows
- Bookmark this file in VS Code (`Ctrl+K Ctrl+K`) so you can return instantly when you need a setting path

</details>

<details>
<summary>Low vision users</summary>

- Increase editor font size (`Ctrl+=`) before scanning the long settings tables -- column values are easier to compare at larger sizes
- Use the Minimap (if sighted enough) or breadcrumbs bar to orient within this large reference file
- High-contrast themes make the table grid lines and code spans easier to distinguish from body text

</details>

<details>
<summary>Sighted users</summary>

- The Table of Contents links jump directly to each section -- click any link to scroll there instantly
- Use `Ctrl+Shift+O` to open the outline view and see all 7 sections as a navigable list
- The settings tables use consistent columns (Setting Path, Values, Default, Description) -- scan the Default column to see what changes from your current setup

</details>

## Table of Contents

1. [Complete Accessibility Settings Reference](#1-complete-accessibility-settings-reference)
2. [Audio Cues - All Options](#2-audio-cues---all-options)
3. [Accessible Diff Viewer - Complete Guide](#3-accessible-diff-viewer---complete-guide)
4. [Screen Reader-Specific Configurations](#4-screen-reader-specific-configurations)
5. [Complete Keyboard Shortcuts](#5-complete-keyboard-shortcuts)
6. [Accessibility Signals Types and Customization](#6-accessibility-signals-types-and-customization)
7. [Settings.json Configuration Examples](#7-settingsjson-configuration-examples)
8. [VS Code 1.120 Chat, Agents Window, and Markdown Diff Updates](#8-vs-code-1120-chat-agents-window-and-markdown-diff-updates)

## 1. Complete Accessibility Settings Reference

All settings can be accessed via Settings UI (`Ctrl+,`) or by editing `settings.json` directly (`Ctrl+Shift+P` → "Open User Settings JSON").

### Core Accessibility Settings

| Setting Path | Values | Default | Description |
| --------------  | --------  | ---------  | -------------  |
| `editor.accessibilitySupport` | `auto`, `on`, `off` | `auto` | Enables screen reader optimizations. `auto` detects NVDA/JAWS/VoiceOver. Set to `on` to force. |
| `editor.accessibilityPageSize` | number (lines) | `10` | Number of lines to read when using Page Up/Down in screen reader mode |
| `editor.guides.bracketPairs` | boolean | `false` | Shows bracket pair guides. Disable for screen readers (visual only). |
| `editor.guides.bracketPairsHorizontal` | boolean | `false` | Shows horizontal bracket guides. Disable for screen readers. |
| `editor.guides.highlightActiveBracketPair` | boolean | `true` | Highlights matching brackets. Not announced by screen readers. |
| `editor.guides.highlightActiveIndentation` | boolean | `true` | Highlights active indentation. Visual only. |
| `editor.guides.indentation` | boolean | `true` | Shows indentation guides. Not useful for screen readers. |
| `editor.hover.enabled` | boolean | `true` | Enables hover popups. Use `Alt+F2` (Accessible View) to read hover content. |
| `editor.minimap.enabled` | boolean | `true` | Shows visual minimap. **Recommended:** Set to `false` for screen readers. |
| `editor.occurrencesHighlight` | boolean | `true` | Highlights occurrences of selected text. Visual only. |
| `editor.renderWhitespace` | `none`, `boundary`, `selection`, `trailing`, `all` | `selection` | Shows whitespace characters. **Recommended:** `none` for screen readers. |
| `editor.wordWrap` | `off`, `on`, `wordWrapColumn`, `bounded` | `off` | Wraps long lines. **Recommended:** `on` for screen readers. |
| `workbench.editor.enablePreview` | boolean | `true` | Opens files in preview mode (single tab). Set to `false` to always open in new tab. |

### Diff and Merge Settings

| Setting Path | Values | Default | Description |
| --------------  | --------  | ---------  | -------------  |
| `diffEditor.codeLens` | boolean | `false` | Shows CodeLens in diff view. Visual only. |
| `diffEditor.diffAlgorithm` | `legacy`, `advanced` | `advanced` | Diff calculation method. `advanced` produces better hunks for screen readers. |
| `diffEditor.ignoreTrimWhitespace` | boolean | `true` | Ignores whitespace changes in diffs. **Recommended:** `true` to reduce noise. |
| `diffEditor.renderSideBySide` | boolean | `true` | Shows diffs side-by-side. Set to `false` for inline view (easier for screen readers). |
| `diffEditor.wordWrap` | `off`, `on`, `inherit` | `inherit` | Word wrap in diff view. `on` recommended for long lines. |
| `merge-conflict.decorators.enabled` | boolean | `true` | Shows merge conflict decorators. Use Accessible Diff instead (`F7`). |

### Terminal Settings

| Setting Path | Values | Default | Description |
| --------------  | --------  | ---------  | -------------  |
| `terminal.integrated.accessibleViewFocusesTerminal` | boolean | `true` | Returns focus to terminal after closing Accessible View. |
| `terminal.integrated.accessibleViewPreserveCursorPosition` | boolean | `false` | Preserves cursor position when opening Accessible View. |
| `terminal.integrated.enableBell` | boolean | `false` | Enables terminal bell sound. **Recommended:** `true` for audio feedback. |
| `terminal.integrated.screenReaderMode` | `auto`, `on`, `off` | `auto` | Optimizes terminal for screen readers. |

### Notification Settings

| Setting Path | Values | Default | Description |
| --------------  | --------  | ---------  | -------------  |
| `accessibility.verbosity.comments` | boolean | `true` | Announces comment threads in code. |
| `accessibility.verbosity.diff-editor` | boolean | `true` | Announces diff editor context. |
| `accessibility.verbosity.editor` | boolean | `true` | Announces editor operations. |
| `accessibility.verbosity.hover` | boolean | `true` | Announces hover content. Use `Alt+F2` for full reading. |
| `accessibility.verbosity.inline-chat` | boolean | `true` | Announces inline chat responses. |
| `accessibility.verbosity.inline-completions` | boolean | `true` | Announces Copilot suggestions. |
| `accessibility.verbosity.keybindings-editor` | boolean | `true` | Announces keybindings editor context. |
| `accessibility.verbosity.notebook` | boolean | `true` | Announces notebook cell operations. |
| `accessibility.verbosity.panel-chat` | boolean | `true` | Announces Copilot Chat panel responses. |
| `accessibility.verbosity.settings-editor` | boolean | `true` | Announces settings editor context. |

## 3. Accessible Diff Viewer - Complete Guide

The Accessible Diff Viewer presents file diffs as a structured, line-by-line list instead of a visual side-by-side view.

### When to Use Accessible Diff Viewer

- Reviewing pull request changes
- Resolving merge conflicts
- Comparing file versions (Timeline view)
- Reviewing Copilot-generated edits
- Any time you need to understand what changed in a file

### Opening Accessible Diff Viewer

| Method | Steps |
| --------  | -------  |
| Keyboard (in diff editor) | Press `F7` to jump to first hunk, `Alt+F2` to open Accessible View |
| Command Palette | `Ctrl+Shift+P` → "Open Accessible Diff Viewer" |
| Automatic | Some contexts open it automatically in screen reader mode |

### Diff Viewer Structure

#### Top-level structure

##### Description

The Accessible Diff Viewer starts with a header showing the file path and change summary. It then shows each hunk (changed section) in order. Each hunk contains: the hunk location (line range), unchanged context lines, the modified, added, or removed lines with their prefix, and more context lines. After all hunks, a footer shows the totals for additions and deletions.

#### Line prefixes

| Prefix | Meaning | Screen Reader Announcement |
| --------  | ---------  | ----------------------------  |
| (no prefix) | Unchanged line (context) | "Unchanged: [line content]" |
| `+` | Added line | "Added: [line content]" or "Line added: [content]" |
| `-` | Removed line | "Removed: [line content]" or "Line removed: [content]" |
| `\|~` | Modified line (original) | "Modified from: [old content]" |
| `\|+` | Modified line (new version) | "Modified to: [new content]" |

### Navigating Hunks

#### Hunk = a block of related changes

| Action | Keyboard |
| --------  | ----------  |
| Jump to next hunk | `F7` |
| Jump to previous hunk | `Shift+F7` |
| Jump to next change | `F8` (in some contexts) |
| Jump to previous change | `Shift+F8` |

### Screen Reader-Specific Navigation

#### NVDA/JAWS

1. Open diff: `Enter` on file in Source Control, or `F7` in an open diff
2. `Alt+F2` to open Accessible Diff Viewer
3. Navigate with `Up/Down Arrow` (line by line)
4. Use `H` key to jump between hunks (each hunk has a heading)
5. `Escape` to close and return to editor

#### VoiceOver

1. `VO+Arrow` to navigate to diff file → `VO+Space` to open
2. `Option+F2` for Accessible Diff Viewer
3. `VO+Arrow` keys to navigate lines
4. `VO+Command+H` to jump between hunk headings
5. `Escape` to close

### Understanding Context Lines

The diff shows 3 unchanged lines before and after each change for context. These are announced as "Unchanged: [content]".

#### Example

```text
Hunk 1 of 3 - lines 42-48

  Unchanged: ## Screen Reader Setup
  Unchanged:
- Removed: This guide covers NVDA only.
+ Added: This guide covers NVDA, JAWS, and VoiceOver.
  Unchanged:
  Unchanged: ### Installing NVDA
```

The unchanged lines help you understand where in the file the change occurred.

### Inline Diff View vs Side-by-Side

#### Inline view (recommended for screen readers)

- All changes in a single editor
- Removed lines followed by added lines
- Easier to navigate with screen reader reading commands

#### Side-by-side view (default, visual)

- Left panel: original file
- Right panel: modified file
- Requires navigating between panels

#### To switch to inline view

1. Open Settings: `Ctrl+,`
2. Search: "diffEditor.renderSideBySide"
3. Uncheck the box (or set to `false` in settings.json)

## 6. Accessibility Signals Types and Customization

Accessibility signals are events that trigger announcements or audio cues. Beyond audio cues, VS Code has verbal announcements for various events.

### Announcement Verbosity Settings

Control how much information VS Code announces:

| Setting | Values | Default | Controls |
| ---------  | --------  | ---------  | ----------  |
| `accessibility.verbosity.chatQuestionCarousel` | `true`, `false` | `true` | ARIA hint in the Agent mode question carousel telling you about `Alt+T` (Focus Terminal) |
| `accessibility.verbosity.diffEditor` | `verbose`, `minimal`, `off` | `verbose` | Diff viewer context announcements |
| `accessibility.verbosity.editor` | `verbose`, `minimal`, `off` | `verbose` | General editor announcements |
| `accessibility.verbosity.hover` | `verbose`, `minimal`, `off` | `verbose` | Hover popup announcements |
| `accessibility.verbosity.inlineCompletions` | `verbose`, `minimal`, `off` | `verbose` | Copilot suggestion announcements |
| `accessibility.verbosity.keyboardShortcuts` | `true`, `false` | `true` | Screen reader navigation hint in the Keyboard Shortcuts search results |
| `accessibility.verbosity.terminal` | `verbose`, `minimal`, `off` | `verbose` | Terminal operation announcements |

**`verbose`:** Announces full context and details  
**`minimal`:** Announces only essential information  
**`off`:** No automatic announcements (use Accessible View manually)

### Custom Announcement Timing

Control when and how often announcements occur:

| Setting | Values | Default | Description |
| ---------  | --------  | ---------  | -------------  |
| `accessibility.signals.debouncePositionChanges` | number (ms) | `500` | Delay before announcing position changes (prevents spam during rapid navigation) |
| `accessibility.signals.onDidChangeFocus` | boolean | `true` | Announce focus changes |
| `accessibility.signals.onDidChangeModelContent` | boolean | `false` | Announce content changes (very verbose) |

### Signal Priorities

When multiple signals occur simultaneously, VS Code prioritizes them:

1. **Errors** (highest priority) - always announced
2. **Warnings** - announced after errors
3. **Completions** - announced if no errors/warnings
4. **Focus changes** - announced last

This prevents overlapping announcements.

## 8. VS Code 1.120 Chat, Agents Window, and Markdown Diff Updates

VS Code 1.120 adds several accessibility-relevant changes for learners who use Copilot, review documentation diffs, or manage agent sessions. For the full Copilot and Agents window workflow, see [Appendix K: VS Code 1.120 Agents Window and Impactful Updates](appendix-k-copilot-reference.md#4a-vs-code-1120-agents-window-and-impactful-updates).

### What Changed

The following table summarizes the 1.120 changes that affect accessible VS Code workflows.

| Feature | Accessibility Impact | Suggested Use |
| ------- | -------------------- | ------------- |
| Agents window, Preview | Gives agent sessions their own window with sessions, chat, customizations, files, and changes | Use Command Palette access, worktree isolation, and Changes panel review |
| Terminal command risk assessment, Experimental | Adds a risk badge and command explanation to some terminal confirmations | Treat as extra context, not permission to skip reading the command |
| Terminal output compression, Preview | Reduces long terminal output sent to chat, which can reduce context noise | Use for large diffs or install logs; ask for raw output when exact text matters |
| Markdown preview for diffs, Preview | Lets documentation diffs render as Markdown instead of only source text | Useful for sighted and low-vision review of headings, lists, links, and tables |
| Plan mode inline control | Lets supported agents show and edit plans inline before implementation | Useful when reviewing an agent plan before file changes start |
| Model picker grouped by provider | Makes model lists easier to scan when many models are available | Keep beginners on Auto; use provider grouping for advanced model selection |
| BYOK token usage and thinking effort | Gives advanced users more visibility and control for bring-your-own-key models | Not needed for beginners; useful for cost and context management |
| Markdown HTML `id` completion and validation | Improves completion and validation for internal links to HTML IDs in Markdown | Helpful when maintaining long workshop docs with many anchors |
| Smart select for Markdown tables | Expands selection from cell to row to whole table | Helpful for keyboard users editing large reference tables |

### Screen Reader Workflow

1. Open the Agents window with **Chat: Open Agents Window** from the Command Palette.
2. Use `Alt+F1` in the focused area to find context-specific accessibility help.
3. Use `F6` and `Shift+F6` to move among major workbench parts.
4. Use `Alt+F2` for Accessible View when chat responses, terminal output, hovers, or diffs are easier to read in a stable buffer.
5. Use `F7` and `Shift+F7` for diff navigation before accepting agent changes.
6. When terminal risk assessment is enabled, listen to the risk label and explanation, then still read the exact command before approving it.

### Low Vision Workflow

1. Set zoom and theme before starting a dense Agents window session.
2. Use modal diff view when side-by-side changes are too compressed.
3. Try Markdown preview diffs for documentation changes where rendered headings, lists, and tables are easier to inspect.
4. Widen the Sessions list, Chat area, and Changes panel as needed before reviewing work.
5. Consider separate Agents window settings if your editor and agent review layouts need different zoom or density.

### Sighted Workflow

1. Use changed-file counts and session status badges as quick scope checks.
2. Open each changed file from the Changes panel before accepting a session result.
3. Use rendered Markdown diffs for documentation PRs and source diffs for syntax-sensitive edits.
4. Use the integrated browser or terminal in the Agents window to validate generated work before committing or merging.

### Settings Reference

The following settings are useful to know when teaching VS Code 1.120 workflows.

| Setting | What It Controls |
| ------- | ---------------- |
| `chat.tools.riskAssessment.enabled` | Shows risk assessment for terminal command confirmations |
| `chat.tools.compressOutput.enabled` | Compresses large terminal output before it is sent to the model |
| `chat.planWidget.inlineEditor.enabled` | Enables inline plan editing for supported agent flows |
| `workbench.diffEditorAssociations` | Can set rendered Markdown preview as the default diff editor for Markdown |
| `extensions.supportAgentsWindow` | Lets you opt specific installed extensions into the Agents window |
| `chat.notifyWindowOnResponseReceived` | Controls OS notifications when chat responses arrive |
| `chat.notifyWindowOnConfirmation` | Controls OS notifications when an agent needs confirmation |

Example setting for rendered Markdown diffs:

```json
{
  "workbench.diffEditorAssociations": {
    "*.md": "vscode.markdown.preview.editor"
  }
}
```
